note: The closest thing to a core fit in this batch, and it fails on one criterion for an instructive reason. He is unambiguously successful — owns a quick-service restaurant, actively scouting a second location, previously a director in fine dining and nightlife, and self-identifies as 'a businessman' three separate times. Income reads as a match on behaviour rather than assertion: he never pleaded constraint, benchmarked the price against personal trainers at roughly $1,000 per ten to twelve sessions and concluded '$6,000 is not a lot of money, but it's also not a little bit of money', which is a valuation posture, not an affordability one. The ask is textbook good-to-great — 182 lb to 170, 'continue getting cut', explicitly not wanting to get bulky — and he is the least deconditioned prospect in the batch, training four to five times a week for three years with 50 to 80 pull-ups before a back session. The miss is neglected_health, and it is a real one rather than a technicality. The stated criterion is that health is the neglected corner of an otherwise ordered life. For this prospect health is the most actively managed thing he has: five-day liquid fasts every other month, a tracked weight history to the pound, a physical therapist on retainer, deliberate deload days, no alcohol. Nothing has been neglected — a system that is running has stopped producing results. That distinction matters commercially, because the playbook is built to make a neglected area painful and there was no neglect here to make painful, which is exactly why Phases 4 and 5 had nothing to grip and the rep ended up reaching for a deathbed frame. Same structural pattern as the Carl Fiorentino call earlier in this batch: a well-qualified buyer whose health is not the neglected variable, sold with a script that assumes it is.
